name: Capacity and server use
answer: These measures show how much of a facility's power and space servers actually use, and how much sits stranded. For AI buildings the question is whether expensive capacity is earning, because idle accelerators and stranded power are paid for either way.

metrics.line: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.
metrics.label: Server utilization rate

metrics.line: Utility power or floor space that is allocated and paid for but cannot be used, because the other of the pair ran out first or airflow limits were reached.
metrics.label: Stranded power and space per cabinet

metrics.line: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.
metrics.label: Floor loading limits

reading.body:
Utilization, stranded capacity, and floor loading decide whether a data center's paid-for power and space actually earn. Idle accelerators and unusable power are paid for either way.

The three measures form a chain. Utilization says how much provisioned compute does real work, measured over time rather than at peak. Stranded power and space is what is allocated and paid for but cannot be used, because the other of the pair ran out first or airflow limits were reached. Floor loading is the structural ceiling on all of it, the weight a raised floor or slab supports per square foot against the weight of the racks actually installed.

For AI specifically, the cost of capacity is high enough that the gap between provisioned and used is the difference between a building that pays for itself and one that does not. Peak figures hide this. A facility can look fully committed and still strand power behind a cabinet that ran out of space, or strand space behind a cabinet that ran out of power.

The data names the measures and what each one tracks. It does not give values, targets, or benchmarks for any of them, so it cannot say what a good utilization rate is or how much stranding is normal.
